prompt: Inside `func sum(nums ...int) int`, what is the type of `nums`?
hint: `show` printed it with `%T`.

choices.text: `int`, holding one argument at a time
choices.why: The function runs once per call, not once per argument; all the arguments arrive together.

choices.text: `[]int`
choices.why: Right. Inside the function a `...T` parameter is always an ordinary slice of `T`, and `%T` printed `[]int`.

choices.text: `[...]int`, an array sized by the call
choices.why: `[...]` sizes an array literal; a variadic parameter is a slice, and `nums == nil` was even true for `show()`.

choices.text: A special variadic type that must be converted before use
choices.why: There is no such type: `sum` ranged over `nums` directly, as over any slice.

prompt: What does `nums` hold when `sum()` is called with no arguments?
hint: `show()` printed four facts about it.

choices.text: Nothing: calling a variadic function with no arguments is a compile error
choices.why: Zero is an allowed number of arguments; `sum()` compiled and returned 0.

choices.text: An empty slice that is not `nil`
choices.why: That is what `sum([]int{}...)` would give; with no arguments at all, `show()` printed `nil=true`.

choices.text: A `nil` slice of length 0
choices.why: Right: `[]int [] len=0 nil=true`. Ranging over it does nothing, so `sum()` is 0.

choices.text: A slice holding one zero, `[0]`
choices.why: No element is invented; the length printed was 0.

prompt: `scores` is a `[]int`. To pass it to `func sum(nums ...int) int`, write `sum(scores___)`.
hint: Without it, the slice is one argument of the wrong type.

prompt: `words` is a `[]string`. Why is `fmt.Println(words...)` refused when `Println` takes `...any`?
hint: What type must a slice passed with `...` have?

choices.text: `Println` accepts only one slice per call, and `words` counts as several
choices.why: There is no such limit; the message says the types differ: `[]string` against `[]any`.

choices.text: Strings cannot be printed through a variadic parameter of type `any`
choices.why: `fmt.Println(words[0], words[1])` works; each string becomes an `any` on its own.

choices.text: `words...` passes the slice itself, and a `[]string` is not a `[]any`
choices.why: Right: `cannot use words (variable of type []string) as []any value`.

choices.text: `...` works only with the standard library's own slices
choices.why: `sum(scores...)` passed a slice declared in `main`; what matters is the element type.

prompt: `func clamp(vals ...int)` sets every element above 100 to 100. A caller does `readings := []int{50, 180}` and then `clamp(readings...)`. What is `readings` afterwards?
hint: With `...`, is a new slice built for the call?

choices.why: Right. `readings...` passes the caller's slice itself, so writing to `vals[1]` writes to the caller's array, as `double(scores...)` did.

choices.text: `[50 180]`, since a function receives copies of its arguments
choices.why: It receives a copy of the slice's three words, and the pointer in them leads to the same array.

choices.text: `[50 180]`, because Go builds a fresh slice for every variadic call
choices.why: Only when the arguments are listed one by one: `double(a, b, c)` left `a`, `b` and `c` alone.

choices.text: It does not compile: a variadic parameter is read-only
choices.why: Nothing makes it read-only; `double` wrote `nums[i] *= 2` and compiled.

prompt: Which of these declarations does the compiler refuse?
hint: Where may the `...` go?

choices.text: `func label(unit string, nums ...int) string`
choices.why: Legal: the variadic parameter is last, so every argument after the first one is a number.

choices.text: `func label(nums ...int, unit string) string`
choices.why: Right: `can only use ... with final parameter`. Nothing could say where `nums` stops.

choices.text: `func label(nums ...int) string`
choices.why: Legal: a function may have a variadic parameter and nothing else, as `sum` did.

choices.text: `func label(unit, sep string, nums ...float64) string`
choices.why: Legal: grouping works before a variadic parameter, and its type may be anything.

prompt: `twice := func(n int) int { return 2 * n }`. What does `fmt.Printf("%T\n", twice)` print?
hint: A function type is its signature without the names.

choices.text: `func`
choices.why: Every function type is more specific than that: what it takes and what it returns are part of it.

choices.text: `int`, the type of what it returns
choices.why: That is the type of `twice(3)`, a call; `twice` alone is the function.

choices.text: `func(int) int`
choices.why: Right. Every function that takes one `int` and returns one has this type, `square` included, which is why both fit `apply`.

choices.text: `func(n int) int`, with the parameter's name
choices.why: Names are not part of a function type; any function taking one `int` and returning one has this type.

prompt: `apply(nums []int, f func(int) int)` is called as `apply(nums, square(2))`. What happens?
hint: What is `square(2)`: a function, or what it returned?

choices.text: `apply` squares every element, starting from 2
choices.why: `square(2)` has already run by the time `apply` is called; what arrives is its result, the `int` 4.

choices.text: It does not compile: `square(2)` is an `int`
choices.why: Right. Brackets call the function; to pass it, write `square` with none.

choices.text: It compiles and every element becomes 4
choices.why: Go does not turn a value into a function that returns it; the types do not match, so the call is refused.

choices.text: It compiles, then panics the first time `apply` calls `f`
choices.why: The mismatch is caught at compile time, before anything runs.

prompt: Match each piece of code to what it is.
hint: Brackets after a name call it.

pairs.right: a named function passed as a value
a call, whose value is an `int`

prompt: `var onDone func()` is declared and later called with `onDone()`, with nothing assigned in between. What happens?
hint: What is the zero value of a function type?

choices.text: Nothing: calling a `nil` function does nothing
choices.why: Some languages skip a missing callback; Go panics, and `not reached` was never printed.

choices.text: The compiler refuses the call
choices.why: Whether a variable holds a function is known only at run time, so it compiles.

choices.text: It compiles, and the call panics with a nil pointer dereference
choices.why: Right: `invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference`, exit status 2. Check `!= nil` first.

choices.text: `onDone` returns its zero value
choices.why: `func()` returns nothing at all, and there is no function there to run.

prompt: You want a registry that maps each callback function to how many times it ran, `map[func()]int`. What does the compiler say?
hint: Which values can be compared with `==`?

choices.text: Nothing: two variables holding the same function compare equal
choices.why: `f == g` was refused even with both holding `square`: functions compare only to `nil`.

choices.text: It compiles, but every lookup misses
choices.why: The refusal comes earlier, at compile time; the map type itself is invalid.

choices.text: It compiles, as long as only named functions are stored, never literals
choices.why: Named or not, the type is `func()`, and the rule is about the type.

choices.text: It refuses the map type: a function is never a valid key
choices.why: Right: `invalid map key type func()`. Lesson 14's rule meets this lesson's.

prompt: `words` is `[]string{"pear", "fig", "banana"}`, sorted with `slices.SortFunc(words, func(a, b string) int { return cmp.Compare(len(a), len(b)) })`. Put the words in the order the sort leaves them.
hint: Negative means `a` comes first.

prompt: `next := counter()` and then `fmt.Println(next(), next(), next())` prints `1 2 3`. Why does the count survive between calls?
hint: Where is `n` declared, and who still refers to it?

choices.text: `n` is a global variable shared by the whole program
choices.why: `n` is local to `counter`; a second `counter()` made a second `n`, and `other()` started at 1.

choices.text: The returned function keeps `n` alive after `counter` ends
choices.why: Right. A closure keeps the variables it uses, for as long as the function value exists.

choices.text: Go remembers the last result of every function
choices.why: Nothing of the kind; `square(3)` gives 9 every time. The state is the variable `n`.

choices.text: `n++` is a static counter, as in C
choices.why: Go has no static locals; the state lives in a variable the closure holds.

prompt:
What does this print?

```go
x := 10
f := func() int { return x * 2 }
x = 5
fmt.Println(f())
```
hint: Does `f` hold `x`, or the value `x` had when `f` was made?

prompt: `d1, _ := account()` and then `_, b2 := account()`. After `d1(50)`, what does `b2()` return?
hint: How many `total` variables exist now?

choices.text: 50, because `deposit` and `balance` always share `total`
choices.why: They share it when they come from the same call. Two calls ran `total := 0` twice.

choices.text: 0: nothing reached the second `total`
choices.why: Right. Each call to `account` makes a new `total`; `d1` changed only the first, and `b2` reads the second.

choices.text: It does not compile: `_` cannot receive a function
choices.why: `_` discards a value of any type, functions included.

choices.text: It panics, because the first `balance` was discarded
choices.why: Discarding one closure does nothing to another; `b2` is a working function over its own `total`.

prompt: With `go 1.21` in `go.mod`, three closures made in `for _, name := range` print `hello, caio` three times. What is the cause?
hint: Count the variables called `name`.

choices.text: The closures are called before the loop starts
choices.why: They were called after it finished, which is exactly when the one variable held its last value.

choices.text: `range` over a slice of strings returns the last element each time
choices.why: The loop did see ana, bia and caio; it stored them all in the same variable, one after another.

choices.text: The loop has one `name`, all three closures hold it, and it ends as "caio"
choices.why: Right. Under `go 1.21` the loop variable is declared once and reassigned on every turn.

choices.text: A bug in Go 1.21's compiler, fixed in 1.22
choices.why: It was the defined behaviour of the language, and go1.27.1 still produces it for a module at `go 1.21`.

prompt: Under a `go` line of 1.22 or later, each turn of a `for` loop declares a ___ loop variable, so `x := x` in its body is no longer needed.
hint: The opposite of one variable reassigned every turn.

prompt:
A module's `go.mod` says `go 1.20`. What does `fs[0](10)` return?

```go
var fs []func(int) int
for i := 1; i <= 3; i++ {
	fs = append(fs, func(n int) int { return n * i })
}
```
hint: Before 1.22 there is one `i`. What value does it hold when the loop has ended?

prompt: Which of these statements about closures are true? Choose every one that is.
hint: Think of `counter`, `account` and `show`.

choices.text: A closure sees changes made to a captured variable after the closure was created
choices.why: True: `show` printed `x is 2` though it was made while `x` was 1.

choices.text: Two closures made in one call can share a variable
choices.why: True: `deposit` and `balance` from one `account()` share `total`.

choices.text: A captured variable is freed when the function that declared it returns
choices.why: False: `n` outlived `counter` and kept counting; lesson 24 says where it lives.

choices.text: Each call to a closure starts its captured variables from their initial values
choices.why: False: `next()` gave 1, 2, 3, so the state carried over between calls.

prompt: `func logf(prefix string, args ...any)` contains `fmt.Println(prefix, args...)`. What does the compiler say?
hint: `args` is already a `[]any`. What else is in that argument list?

choices.text: Nothing: `args` is a `[]any`, exactly what `...any` wants
choices.why: The type is right, but `args...` must be the whole variadic part, and `prefix` sits in front of it.

choices.text: It refuses it: `args...` cannot follow a listed value
choices.why: Right: `too many arguments in call to fmt.Println`, `have (string, []any...)`. The slice is passed as it is, so nothing else can join it.

choices.text: It compiles and prints `prefix` followed by the slice in brackets
choices.why: That would be `fmt.Println(prefix, args)`, without the dots, which does compile.

choices.text: It refuses the declaration `args ...any`, since `any` cannot be variadic
choices.why: `Println` itself is declared `a ...any`; any type can follow the dots.
